A SOAP web service exchanges structured messages according to the Simple Object Access Protocol. SOAP defines an application-level messaging contract above the transport and is commonly carried through HTTP rather than replacing HTTP's network role.

The contract can standardize operations and message structure across consumers, but its additional envelope and service conventions are useful only when both sides need that formal interoperability.

A social bot content feature is derived from the language and symbols used in an account's posts. Word usage, parts of speech, entities, hashtags, links, and repetition can characterize automated production.

Content features capture what an account says, but language varies by topic, community, and time. Robust detection separates automation signals from ordinary topical differences.

A social bot friend feature summarizes properties of the accounts connected to a focal user. Aggregates over followers or friends can expose an unusual social environment even when the focal profile appears ordinary.

These features extend detection beyond self-reported attributes. Sampling limits, private accounts, and coordinated manipulation can affect the reliability of friend-based summaries.

A social bot is an automated or partially automated account that participates in an online social system. Bots can provide benign services or manipulate attention, conversation, and apparent consensus.

Detection is difficult because behavior ranges from simple automation to coordinated, human-like activity. Feature engineering combines account, content, temporal, and network evidence rather than relying on a single visible cue.

A social bot network feature describes structural or interaction relationships involving an account. Retweet, mention, and hashtag co-occurrence networks provide different views of how it participates in information flow.

Network measures can expose coordination, centrality, and neighborhood patterns. Each network definition encodes a different behavior, so combining them requires attention to scale and meaning.

A social bot temporal feature summarizes when and how regularly an account acts. Posting intervals, daily rhythms, bursts, and response timing can expose scheduling or machine-speed behavior.

Automation does not always mean constant or perfectly regular activity, and humans can also show routines. Temporal evidence is therefore more reliable as part of a multi-family representation.

A social bot user feature derives from profile and account attributes such as age, description, counts, or interface settings. These variables summarize how an account presents itself and its accumulated platform activity.

User features are inexpensive and interpretable, but sophisticated bots can imitate normal profiles. They are strongest when combined with behavioral and relational evidence.

A social contextual factor is relationship or interaction information that conditions a user's behavior. The book groups rich social evidence into [[Individual Preference]] and [[Interpersonal Influence]], derived from content, user-item activity, user-user activity, and explicit relations.

Context makes recommendation more than a lookup of similar items. It explains how an identical item can receive different responses depending on receivers, senders, and their prior history.

A social explanation of an AI decision treats explanation as an answer given by one party to another in a particular context. The affected person usually asks not for every calculation, but why this outcome occurred, what evidence mattered, how it compares with alternatives, and what can be challenged.

Explanations are therefore audience-sensitive and connected to responsibility. A technical account for a developer, an audit record for a regulator, and a reason given to an applicant may all be valid at different levels. [[Explainable AI]] succeeds ethically when it supports understanding and action rather than merely increasing the volume of disclosed information.

A social honeypot is a legitimate-looking account created to attract suspicious interactions. Accounts that send deceptive information or malicious links to it become candidates for labeling and later supervised detection.

Honeypots obtain labels cheaply but passively, so collection may take a long time. They also emphasize malicious positive examples and require another method to represent normal accounts accurately.

A social networking service provides a shared online environment for identities, relationships, messages, media, and continuing updates. Its value grows from the interactions and content contributed by participants.

These services descend from bulletin boards, chat rooms, Usenet, and commercial online communities. Centralized platforms combine those functions at scale while controlling access to much of the resulting data.

A social robot is an embodied system that interacts with people through speech, movement, gaze, expression, and spatial behavior. Its physical presence makes [[Nonverbal Communication]] part of the interface.

Unlike a screen-only assistant, it must locate speakers, orient sensors, coordinate motion with dialog, and behave safely in shared space. Embodiment intensifies both social expectations and technical failure modes.

A social virtual assistant is designed to participate in relationship-oriented interaction as well as complete instrumental tasks. It uses conversational style, memory, and an [[Assistant Personality]] to create continuity across encounters.

Social behavior can improve engagement, but apparent empathy or companionship may encourage users to attribute abilities the system does not possess. Design should keep the assistant's actual limits legible.

A societal cloud serves people connected by a common geography, language, institution, hobby, industry, or civic interest. It can provide shared communication, documents, information, analysis, or services within that community boundary.

Aggregated and de-identified data can support group-level analysis, while the service can broker more individualized capabilities for members. The shared purpose must not be treated as blanket permission to expose personal information.

A soft authentication token is a software-generated credential used to demonstrate possession of an enrolled device or secret. It commonly produces a time-limited or challenge-based value that supplements [[Password Authentication]].

As a possession factor in [[Multi-Factor Authentication]], it can prevent a password alone from granting access. Its protection still depends on device security, enrollment integrity, recovery procedures, and resistance to real-time interception.

A software code feature measures static properties of a software artifact, such as size, complexity, coupling, or organization. These product metrics summarize what the code is like at a selected revision.

Code features are interpretable and widely available, but they provide only a snapshot. Combining them with process features captures how the artifact reached that state.

A software integration, deployment or release means that the software is made available to users. Deployment involves setting up database and server configurations, procuring necessary cloud computing resources and monitoring the production environment. Development teams often use [infrastructure as code (IaC)](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/infrastructure-as-code) solutions to automate the provisioning of resources. Such automations help simplify scaling and reduce costs.

Often organizations use preliminary releases, such as beta tests, before releasing a new product to the public. These tests release the product to a selected group of users for testing and feedback and enable teams to identify and address unforeseen issues with the software before a public release.

A software process feature summarizes how code has been developed or changed. Commit frequency, developer activity, prior defects, ownership, and churn are examples.

Process measures can reveal risk that static code metrics miss because unstable history and coordination matter. Their calculation requires a clear time window and careful identity and repository cleaning.

A software system tends to reflect the communication structure of the organization that builds it. Teams that coordinate through particular boundaries often produce components and interfaces with similar boundaries.

This relationship can be used deliberately by aligning team responsibilities with a desired architecture. If ignored, organizational silos may become accidental technical dependencies that make integration and change harder.

A solar array interconnects [[Solar Module]]s to supply a chosen voltage, current, and power. Series-connected modules raise operating voltage; parallel-connected branches increase output current. The source sizes these counts from nominal module ratings and required generator voltage and current. Array output also reflects mismatch, wiring, temperature, and the fraction of total exposed area actually covered by cells.

A solar cell is an individual semiconductor device that uses a [[P-N Junction]] to deliver electrical power from incident sunlight. Light generates carriers in the junction, while contacts take the resulting current to an external circuit. Cells have material-dependent voltage and illumination- and area-dependent current. They can be wired into a [[Solar Module]] for higher useful voltage or current.

A solar chimney plant heats ground-level air beneath a transparent cover. Warm air rises through a tall chimney because of its density difference from cooler air, and the resulting flow drives an air turbine and generator. The source calls this semi-direct: sunlight creates the air flow, but a moving turbine still converts its mechanical energy into electricity. Chimney height and collecting area affect output.

A solar collector absorbs incident sunlight and transfers useful heat to a fluid such as water or air. Heat can serve a task directly or feed a later power cycle. The source groups collectors by operating temperature and distinguishes flat-plate units, which can use diffuse light, from focusing units that concentrate [[Beam Solar Radiation]]. Useful heat is incident absorbed energy minus optical and thermal losses.

A solar module connects several [[Solar Cell]]s in a series-parallel wiring arrangement and encloses them under a rigid transparent cover. The number of cells in series helps set voltage, while parallel paths increase current. Contacts, cover, frame, and exposed gaps distinguish module performance from that of an individual cell. Modules are the repeatable building blocks of a [[Solar Array]].

A solar pond uses a vertical salt-concentration gradient to keep warm dense water at the bottom instead of letting it circulate to the cooler surface. Its middle nonconvective layer suppresses heat loss while the bottom layer stores solar heat. Hot lower water can drive an organic-fluid power cycle or provide process heat, and cool upper water can serve the condenser. The pond is both collector and storage medium.

A solar thermal power plant collects sunlight as heat, transfers it to a working fluid, and runs a thermodynamic power cycle. It is different from a [[Solar Cell]], which generates electricity in a junction without a heat-engine stage. The source's high-temperature plants use concentrating collectors, receivers, heat transport, and often storage to handle variable solar input and demand.

A solar tower plant uses a field of tracking [[Heliostat]]s to direct [[Beam Solar Radiation]] to one high-mounted [[Solar Central Receiver]]. The receiver heats steam, air, liquid metal, or another primary fluid; its heat then feeds a power cycle. Field reflectivity, interception, receiver loss, and heat transport determine useful power. It is a point-focus alternative to line-focus parabolic troughs.

A solar-cell current-voltage curve records how output current changes as operating voltage changes under a particular illumination level. It marks open-circuit voltage, short-circuit current, and an interior operating point where their product is greatest. Comparing curves at different radiation levels shows why the available electrical output of a [[Solar Cell]] changes with sunlight. See [[Solar Cell Maximum Power Point]].

A solar-thermal system model combines collection, storage, fluid circulation, distribution, controls, and auxiliary heat rather than rating a collector alone. Weather and load change over minutes or hours, while useful delivery totals may be needed over months or years. The source recommends numerical simulation because component equations are nonlinear and continually changing; repeated time-step calculations reveal whole-system behavior.

A solid oxide fuel cell uses a ceramic oxide-ion conducting [[Fuel Cell Electrolyte]] and porous metal-ceramic electrodes. Oxygen-side ions travel through the ceramic and react with hydrogen or carbon monoxide at the fuel electrode. The source describes high-temperature operation and use in industrial or cogeneration plants, where usable exhaust heat can complement the electrical output. It contrasts with low-temperature polymer-membrane cells.

A solution of an equation is a value for the [[Unknown Variable]] that makes both sides equal when substituted into the original equation. An equation may have one solution, several solutions, no solution, or be an identity with every permitted value as a solution.

A proposed result is not complete until its domain restrictions are respected. Multiplying, dividing, factoring, or cross multiplying can hide excluded values or introduce candidates that do not satisfy the original form. [[Equation Verification]] distinguishes valid solutions from such extraneous candidates.

A solvable group has a chain from the identity subgroup to the whole group in which each subgroup is normal in the next and each successive quotient is abelian. Abelian groups are therefore solvable.

The symmetric group Sₙ is not solvable for n at least five.

A sort key is the feature or combination of features used to compare [[Data Record|records]] and determine their order. The key must provide an ordering that the [[Sorting Algorithm]] can apply.

A key may be atomic, such as one identifier treated as a single value, or composite, such as sender followed by delivery date. Composite keys order tied values from an earlier field by consulting the next field.

A sorting algorithm rearranges a collection of [[Data Record|records]] into an order determined by a [[Sort Key]]. Its output must be a [[Permutation]] of the input: every original record is retained, with only the order changed.

Different algorithms offer different advantages. [[Insertion Sort]] accepts streamed input, [[Radix Sort]] distributes records by key parts, [[Quicksort]] is fast in typical in-memory use, and [[Merge Sort]] supports systematic division and parallel work.

A sound event handle identifies one live instance of a [[Game Audio Event]]. Through the handle, game code can pause, stop, reposition, change parameters, or query playback without owning the middleware object's raw lifetime directly.

The handle becomes invalid when playback completes or the instance is released. A sound wrapper should check validity so delayed gameplay code does not manipulate an event that the audio system has already removed.

A source code repository records versioned application files and provides the revision consumed by the continuous-integration pipeline. A pushed change can serve as the trigger and gives the resulting build an identifiable source state.

The repository is the pipeline's starting contract: build definitions, application code, tests, and relevant deployment scripts must agree at that revision. Generated artifacts are outputs and should not obscure which source produced them.

A source resolving set is a collection of observed nodes whose graph-distance patterns can distinguish candidate rumor sources. Each candidate receives a vector of distances to the observers, and distinct vectors make the origins identifiable.

For multiple sources, the objective is to find a small resolving set under source-count constraints. Greedy approximation can make the combinatorial search practical on general graphs.

A space-time horizon graph gives each aggregated geographic zone a compact temporal strip and encodes deviations from a reference through layered color bands. It allows many zonal series to be aligned vertically, revealing when and where values depart from the local average. The technique depends on [[Spatial Aggregation by Zone]] and sacrifices exact magnitudes and within-zone geography for a dense comparison of temporal patterns.

A space-time level plot displays selected layers of a [[Space-Time Raster]] as colored map panels. Each panel preserves the complete spatial grid for one time, and a shared color key supports comparison among snapshots. The approach exposes both geographic pattern and change but is limited by page area: as the number of layers grows, panels become too small. Temporal aggregation or animation provides alternative views.

A space-time map series displays the spatial observations for several time indexes as repeated map panels. Each panel retains two-dimensional geography, making local differences and moving patterns visible, but page space limits the number of times that can be shown. Shared symbols, class boundaries, and extents support comparison. A [[Space-Time XT Plot]] or time-series view provides a more comprehensive account of long temporal sequences.

A space-time raster box plot summarizes the distribution of cell values at each time or temporal group using quartiles, a median, and outlier conventions. It supports compact comparison across many periods but does not show multiple modes or geographic arrangement. A [[Space-Time Raster Violin Plot]] adds distribution shape, while the original maps identify where unusually high or low cells occur.

A space-time raster density plot estimates a smooth distribution of cell values for each selected temporal group. It can make multiple modes and gradual distribution changes easier to compare than a binned histogram. Bandwidth controls smoothness and can create or erase apparent structure. Since the plot aggregates across cells, it should be read alongside maps that preserve the geography of the [[Space-Time Raster]].

A space-time raster histogram groups cell values by a time-derived condition and displays their frequency distributions in separate panels. Monthly histograms can reveal seasonal shifts, spread, skewness, or multiple modes that maps alone do not summarize. Because cells are pooled across geography, the display loses location. It therefore complements [[Space-Time Raster Small Multiples]] rather than explaining where each part of the distribution occurs.

A space-time raster is a sequence of aligned raster layers whose cells describe a field at successive times. It forms a three-dimensional array with two spatial dimensions and one temporal dimension. A [[Space-Time Level Plot]] shows selected snapshots, while [[Hovmoller Diagram|Hovmoller diagrams]] or time-series reductions aggregate one spatial direction. No single two-dimensional display preserves every relationship in the full array.

A space-time raster scatterplot matrix compares cell values between every pair of selected raster times or temporal aggregates. Each point represents the same cell in two layers, so linear or nonlinear patterns show how spatial values persist or change. Diagonal density summaries describe each layer's distribution. The matrix grows quickly with layer count and does not show where deviating cells are located.

A space-time raster violin plot combines a density-shaped silhouette with box-plot summaries for the cells belonging to each temporal group. It reveals changes in central tendency, spread, and multimodality, such as recurring clear-sky and overcast modes. The shape depends on density bandwidth and ignores cell locations. [[Space-Time Raster Small Multiples]] are therefore needed to connect the distribution back to geography.

A space-time XT plot places spatial locations or zones on the horizontal axis, time on the vertical axis, and observed value in color. Each column traces one location through time, enabling comparison of persistent levels and shared temporal events across a network. The display preserves the location identities but not their two-dimensional geographic arrangement, so a [[Space-Time Map Series]] supplies complementary spatial context.

A space-wide point time series uses time as the row index and gives each point location its own value column. It is created by reshaping [[Long-Format Space-Time Data]] and supports multivariate temporal plotting. To construct a full point space-time object, its values can be transposed and vectorized so the spatial index varies fastest within each time. The wide form makes missing location-time combinations explicit.

A space-wide time series stores each spatial zone or location as a separate variable and each time as a shared observation row. It converts a space-time dataset into a multivariate temporal form, enabling conventional line and horizon plots. The representation preserves temporal comparison among locations but treats geographic adjacency as metadata rather than visible position. Maps are needed to restore that spatial relationship.

A sparse autoencoder adds a constraint that encourages only a small proportion of hidden units to be active for any input. The network may therefore use a wide hidden layer without learning a trivial identity representation.

Sparse activation promotes selective, parts-like features and can improve interpretability. The strength and form of the sparsity penalty determine the balance between accurate reconstruction and specialized codes.

A sparse document vector represents a text using weights for only the terms that occur, commonly after frequency and inverse-document-frequency transformations. Most vocabulary coordinates are zero, making sparse storage and computation essential.

Cosine-like similarity often focuses on term distribution rather than document magnitude. High dimensionality, synonymy, polysemy, and common background language can still obscure the topical structure sought by clustering.

A sparse matrix is a [[Matrix]] in which most entries are zero. Instead of reserving memory for every position, an implementation can store only the coordinates and values of nonzero entries.

The web's [[Hyperlink Matrix]] is sparse because each page links to only a tiny fraction of all pages. Exploiting that structure makes calculations over a graph containing billions of nodes far more practical in time and storage.

A sparse model matrix represents predictors numerically while storing only nonzero entries. It is efficient for one-hot encoded categorical data because most indicator columns are zero for any record.

The encoding rules must be learned from training data and applied consistently to validation, test, and future scoring records.

A sparse space-time grid stores only the non-missing combinations from an underlying lattice of spatial features and observation times. It avoids allocating every cell of a [[Full Space-Time Grid]] when many combinations are absent while retaining the idea of shared spatial and temporal indexes. In the `spacetime` package, STS and [[STSDF Object|STSDF]] represent this layout.

A spatial display is built on decisions about what kind of geographic phenomenon is being represented. [[R Spatial Data Structures]] separates discrete objects from continuous fields. Points, lines, and polygons describe features with identifiable locations or boundaries, while rasters divide an extent into cells to approximate quantities or categories distributed across space. Simple-feature tables connect each geometry to ordinary attributes, and multilayer raster structures align variables or times over the same grid. None of these coordinates are self-explanatory: a coordinate reference system states how they relate to the Earth, and its projection determines which geometric properties a flat map preserves or distorts.

Point observations lead naturally to [[Proportional Symbol Mapping]]. A proportional symbol map places an area-scaled mark at each location so magnitude and geography remain visible together. Because circle area rather than radius must be proportional to the value, mathematical scaling matters, and perceptual correction may be used cautiously when area differences are systematically underestimated. Graduated symbols instead group values into a small number of classes, allowing range grading to choose reliably distinct sizes. Fisher-Jenks breaks can follow clusters in the distribution, while a well-constructed legend exposes the mapping from numbers to sizes. Labels identify selected places, and interpolation can transform discrete samples into a continuous surface, although that analytical model requires validation beyond the appearance of the resulting map.

Regional attributes are organized by [[Choropleth Mapping]]. A choropleth fills each polygon and thereby treats its value as applying throughout the region, which makes normalized rates or proportions generally more defensible than raw totals. Sequential palettes express ordered magnitude, while qualitative palettes distinguish categories without implying rank. Classed maps simplify values into intervals, forcing choices about class count and boundaries. Quantiles allocate similar numbers of regions to each color; natural breaks instead follow the observed distribution. Unclassed maps preserve a continuous scale but exceed the eye's ability to recover fine numeric differences. Small multiples support comparison across times or variables, and bivariate choropleths combine two attributes only when a restrained two-dimensional legend remains readable.

Continuous and directional phenomena require the encodings collected in [[Raster and Vector Field Mapping]]. Quantitative rasters map each cell through an ordered or diverging palette, with row and column summaries providing reduced views of broad spatial gradients. Diverging colors need a meaningful neutral reference, not merely a wide numeric range. Categorical rasters decode integer values through attribute tables and use qualitative colors, while bivariate rasters combine category and magnitude at the cost of additional visual complexity. Hill shading derives apparent relief from elevation and can supply physical context beneath a translucent theme. Vector fields add direction: arrows show local magnitude and orientation at samples, whereas streamlines reveal the continuous structure suggested by the field. Neither display should be so dense that its flow becomes texture.

A spatial feature is a geographic entity represented by geometry together with descriptive attributes. A feature may be a point, line, polygon, or a multipart collection of these forms. In the [[Simple Feature]] model, each row of a data frame represents one feature and a geometry list-column stores its shape. Mapping joins the feature's attributes to visual properties while its geometry determines position and extent.

A spatial field treats a variable as potentially defined at every location in a region, even when it is observed only at a finite set of samples. Elevation, temperature, and solar radiation are common examples. A raster discretizes the field into cells as [[Raster Data]], while [[Point-Surface Interpolation]] estimates unsampled locations from point observations. Field maps emphasize spatial pattern rather than individual named objects.

A spatial tooltip displays a short attribute value or label when the pointer reaches a map feature. It provides detail on demand without permanently covering nearby points or regions. Because tooltips disappear, they are poorly suited to comparing many locations or communicating essential categories. Selection tolerance, touch support, and unambiguous feature highlighting help users understand which geometry supplied the displayed information.

A spatial trajectory is an ordered sequence of locations associated with successive times, representing the movement of an entity through space. Its position and time are linked rather than forming all possible combinations of independent spatial and temporal indexes. The `spacetime` package uses STT and [[STTDF Object|STTDF]] for simple trajectories. Speed or direction can be derived only after accounting for time intervals and the coordinate system.

A spatiotemporal point symbol represents a location's value at one time through size, color, or both. Repeating the mapping across panels or animation lets the same station be followed through time. Size should use area-based scaling, and color classes must remain stable across frames. If both channels encode the same value, redundancy can reinforce magnitude; if they encode different variables, the legend must explain their combination.

A spatiotemporal time-series plot draws a separate temporal trajectory for each spatial location or zone in a shared panel or aligned set of panels. It emphasizes timing, common peaks, and persistent differences but removes map position. Thin transparent lines can reveal the network's overall behavior. A [[Space-Time XT Plot]] may make long-duration level differences easier to scan, while maps identify where those locations are.

A special factorization recognizes a polynomial as one side of a standard algebraic identity. Common patterns include a difference of squares, a perfect-square trinomial, and sums or differences of cubes.

Recognition can shorten work and reveal further factors. For example,

$$x^4-81=(x^2-9)(x^2+9)=(x-3)(x+3)(x^2+9).$$

The first identity exposes another difference of squares, so factorization continues in stages. A pattern should be verified against all signs and exponents rather than applied from visual resemblance alone.

A speech frame is a short segment of audio treated as approximately stable for acoustic analysis. Speech recognizers commonly analyze overlapping intervals on the order of about ten milliseconds.

Each frame is transformed by [[Speech Feature Extraction]] into measurements such as filter-bank energies. A sequence of frames lets an [[Acoustic Model]] track how speech evolves over time.

A speech recognition grammar specifies the words and phrase patterns a recognizer should consider in a constrained interaction. Restricting the search space can improve accuracy when the next valid responses are predictable.

A [[Directed Prompt]] can establish such expectations for the user and system. Broad assistants need more open statistical models because their possible utterances cannot be enumerated compactly.

A speech synthesizer generates the acoustic waveform for a planned sequence of speech sounds and prosodic targets. It may concatenate recorded units, predict acoustic parameters, or generate audio directly with a neural model.

The synthesizer is the final computational stage of [[Text-to-Speech]] before digital-to-analog conversion and playback. Its output quality depends on the linguistic and prosodic information supplied upstream.

A speech-to-text service exposes [[Automatic Speech Recognition]] through a network interface. A device sends captured audio to a remote system and receives a transcript that another assistant component can interpret.

Centralized services can use large models and compute resources, but they introduce latency, connectivity, and privacy concerns. Local [[Wake Word]] detection can limit transmission to audio that follows a likely activation.

A sphere with center $(h,k,l)$ and radius $r$ is the set of points satisfying

$$(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2+(z-l)^2=r^2.$$

The equation fixes the three-dimensional distance from every surface point to the center, extending the planar [[Circle Equation]] by one coordinate.

A sphere-AABB intersection test finds the point on an axis-aligned box closest to the sphere center by clamping each coordinate to the box interval. The sphere intersects when the squared distance to that closest point is no greater than the squared radius.

This reduces a mixed-shape test to [[Point-in-AABB Test|clamping]] plus a distance comparison. It also supplies a useful closest point for later response calculations.

A spherical triangle is a region on a sphere bounded by three arcs of [[Great Circle]]s. Its side lengths are measured as central angles, and its vertex angles are angles between the corresponding great-circle planes. Unlike a Euclidean triangle, its interior-angle sum is greater than $180^\circ$.

A spike is a timeboxed backlog item whose primary result is knowledge. A team uses it to research, experiment, or prototype when uncertainty prevents responsible estimation or design.

The spike answers a stated question and ends at its time limit. Any production feature revealed by the work is planned separately, preventing investigation from silently becoming unbounded implementation.

A spiking neuron maintains an internal activation potential that changes as input pulses arrive and decays when they do not. It emits an output event only when the potential crosses a threshold. Timing therefore matters: enough inputs must occur within a suitable window to trigger a spike.

Kelleher contrasts this event-driven unit with a standard artificial neuron that computes an activation from the inputs at each processing step. In [[Neuromorphic Computing]], sparse firing can reduce repeated activity and energy use. It is a hardware-oriented computational model inspired by biological signaling, not a claim that all neural-network tasks are better expressed with spikes.

A spiral model combines elements of both waterfall and iterative approaches. Like the waterfall model, a spiral development model delineates a clear series of steps. But it also breaks down the process into a series of loops or “phases” that give development teams more flexibility to analyze, test and modify software throughout the process.  
  
The visual representation of these models takes the form of a spiral, with the beginning planning and requirements gathering step as the center point. Each loop or phase represents the entire software delivery cycle. At the start of each new phase, teams can modify requirements, review testing and adjust any code as needed. The spiral model offers risk-management benefits and is ideal for large, complex projects.

A spline camera moves along a smooth curve defined by control points. It is useful for cutscenes, introductions, and guided views where authored motion should pass through a sequence of locations without sharp corners.

Position can be evaluated from a [[Catmull-Rom Spline]], while orientation may follow a separate target or interpolated path. Timing determines how quickly the camera traverses each curve segment.

A split-complementary scheme begins with one base hue and replaces its direct complement with the two hues adjacent to that complement. It preserves noticeable contrast while distributing it across a less confrontational relationship.

The base hue can establish the environmental field while the two opposing hues separate different accents or gameplay categories. Value and saturation control keep the three colors hierarchical instead of equally dominant.

A spring follow camera treats the desired follow position as an anchor connected to the actual camera by a damped spring. Displacement creates a restoring force, while damping reduces oscillation.

The resulting lag smooths sudden target motion and can make the view feel more natural than a rigid [[Follow Camera]]. Spring constants and damping must be tuned so responsiveness is preserved without jitter or prolonged overshoot.

A Sprint Goal is the coherent outcome a team intends to achieve during a [[Sprint]]. It gives the selected backlog work a shared purpose and supports trade-offs when details change.

For a game team, a strong goal describes playable value or the reduction of an important risk. Completing unrelated discipline tasks is weaker because it postpones integration and obscures whether the player experience improved.

A Sprint is a fixed one-to-three-week interval in which a [[Scrum Team]] pursues a [[Sprint Goal]] and produces a usable [[Product Increment]]. Its stable duration creates a regular opportunity to inspect the product and adapt both plans and practices.

A Sprint contains planning, daily coordination, development, review, and retrospective work. It is not merely a deadline for a batch of disconnected tasks.

A Sprint reset ends and replans a Sprint when its goal has become obsolete or impossible. Incomplete backlog items return to the Product Backlog and the team begins planning again from the changed reality.

A reset is deliberately rare because it discards coordination and creates overhead. Ordinary discovery should be handled by adapting the Sprint plan while preserving the goal.

A Sprint Retrospective inspects how a team created value and identifies a small improvement to try in the next Sprint. A simple format asks what to stop, start, and continue, then assigns and tracks the chosen action.

The event focuses on the working system, relationships, tools, and practices. It turns [[Continuous Improvement]] into an explicit recurring responsibility.

A sprite component attaches a two-dimensional image and drawing behavior to a [[Game Actor]]. It derives its position, scale, and rotation from the actor while storing presentation-specific data such as texture, dimensions, and draw order.

The renderer maintains sprite components in sorted order so the [[2D Painter's Algorithm]] produces the intended layering. An animated specialization can change texture regions over time without altering the actor model.
